title: Revisiting Value Iteration: Unified Analysis of Discounted and Average-Reward Cases
claim: Empirical convergence is geometric and far faster than the classical worst-case rate bound, with the gap widening as the problem becomes harder.
layout: 2 side-by-side log-scale line plots, shared legend below, solid vs dashed curves
description: Two side-by-side semilog line plots. Panel A is titled 'Constructed MDP' and panel B is 'Random MDP'. The x-axis is iteration t from 0 to 20. The y-axis is normalized span seminorm on a log scale. In panel A it runs from 1 down to about 1e-8. In panel B it runs from 1 down to about 1e-4. Four colors stand for discount factors 0.8 (blue), 0.9 (orange), 0.99 (green) and 0.999 (red). Solid curves with round markers show the empirical span, which falls steeply and almost linearly in log scale. Dashed lines of the same colors show the theoretical gamma^t bound, which decays slowly or stays flat near 1 for large gamma. The wide gap between solid and dashed curves is the main visual point. A two-row legend sits below both panels.
caption: Normalized span seminorm versus iteration t (log scale) for four discount factors γ ∈ {0.8, 0.9, 0.99, 0.999}. Subfigure (A) shows an MDP used as an example in Section 1; a detailed description is given in Appendix A. Subfigure (B) shows a random MDP with 10 states, 1 to 4 actions on each state, and random rewards. Solid curves are the empirical spans (each normalized by its initial value). Across both MDPs, as γ approaches 1, the empirical spans decay rate approaches a geometrical convergence with a rate significantly faster than 1.
abstract: While Value Iteration (VI) is one of the most fundamental algorithms in Reinforcement Learning, its theoretical convergence guarantees still exhibit a persistent mismatch with empirical behavior. In the discounted-reward case, classical theory guarantees geometric convergence with rate $Î³$, while in the average-reward case recent work suggests that only sublinear convergence can be expected. In practice, however, VI is often observed to converge significantly faster. In this work, we show through a unified geometry-based analysis that, under an assumption of a unique and unichain optimal policy, (i) convergence is geometric in both the discounted- and average-reward settings and (ii) the convergence rate is faster than previous analyses suggest.
